title: The Hidden Blade
full_review:
Director Yoji Yamada's "The Twilight Samurai," a 2002 Oscar nominee, was notable for his rich character development and sociological detail.

This follow-up, "The Hidden Blade" (Tartan), the second in a trilogy, has all the virtues of the first. It's a terrific 19th-century drama about honorable samurai Munezo Katagiri (Masatoshi Nagase) who is asked to hunt down and kill his friend, Yaichiro Hazama (Yukiyoshi Ozawa), who has turned renegade against the ruling shogunate.

The two men studied together under Master Toda (Min Tanaka) who has imparted secret "esoteric" swordplay techniques, including the titular "hidden blade," to Katagiri alone.

There's a romantic subplot involving a former family domestic, Kie (Takako Matsu), whom Katagiri rescues from an abusive family and takes into his home, but for whom he cannot declare his feelings.

Yamada paints a vivid picture of changing times, and the onslaught of Western-style artillery and tactics facing down the traditional Japanese formal style, exemplified by an instructor from faraway Edo who tries to teach the old-guard samurai how to use guns and cannons. It's clear he's facing a hopeless task, disdainfully bemoaning his lot in a "backwater."

The performances are very fine indeed. Besides the principals already mentioned, there is a gallery of marvelous parts, including the callous chief retainer (Ken Ogata), who commits an immoral act which greatly offends Katagiri's sense of honor; Hazama's crafty wife (Reiko Takashima), who begs Katagiri to spare her husband's life, and even pathetically offers her body in exchange; and Katagiri's childlike sister (Tomoko Tabata).

The evocation of the passing age of the samurai code, in the face of the more ruthless Western techniques is vividly conveyed. Making cultural allowances for such practices as hara-kiri (suicide), the film has a strong moral center, and a strong anti-violence message.

Subtitles.

This film contains relatively moderate violence with brief bloodshed and gore, a murder without retribution, discreet sexual themes and a couple of mild expletives. The USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is A-III -- adults. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is R -- restricted. Under 17 requires accompanying parent or adult guardian.
